 Bucks, Lakers, Grizzlies Reportedly Exploring Trades
 By Luke Adams |
 at October 15, 2026 9:02 am 
 The Bucks , Lakers , and Grizzlies are all exploring the trade market for potential deals as they look to address their roster crunches, according to Jake Fischer of The Stein Line and Bleacher Report ( Twitter link ).
 Milwaukee, Los Angeles, and Memphis are the only three NBA teams currently carrying more than 15 players on fully guaranteed contracts. They have until Monday, the day before the regular season tips off, to make the necessary moves to reduce their roster to 15 players on standard deals.
 The Bucks actually have 17 players on standard contracts, though Pete Nance ’s minimum salary is non-guaranteed, making him one of the two probable odd men out in Milwaukee.
 Veteran swingman Caris LeVert is another player to watch for the Bucks, since he’s on an expiring $14.8MM contract and was acquired in a trade that also netted the club a pair of second-round picks (in other words, he wasn’t the primary target in the deal). LeVert has struggled in three preseason games for Milwaukee, scoring just three points on 1-of-7 shooting in 37 minutes while committing seven turnovers.
 2024 first-round pick Dalton Knecht has been considered the most likely release candidate for the Lakers if they don’t make a trade before the season begins. He fell out of the rotation in his second NBA season and hasn’t been effective in three preseason contests, scoring 11 points on 3-of-11 shooting with six turnovers in 40 total minutes of action.
 The Lakers have reportedly explored the possibility of making a consolidation trade to clear their roster logjam. In that scenario, Knecht, Jaden Hardy , and Jarred Vanderbilt would likely rank among the team’s top trade candidates.
 As for the Grizzlies, while they have 16 players on fully guaranteed salaries, a 17th player – Jaylen Wells – is on track to make the standard roster despite not having a guaranteed deal, which means the team will need to trade or waive two players in the coming days. Offseason trade acquisitions Kris Murray and Micah Peavy have been viewed as possible odd men out if Memphis doesn’t make a trade.
 As Fischer and Marc Stein ( Twitter link ) point out, the Hornets and Mavericks are two other clubs worth monitoring, since they would each have to part with a player on a guaranteed contract in order to keep locker-room leaders Pat Connaughton and Dwight Powell , respectively.
 While Connaughton’s minimum salary is fully non-guaranteed, the veteran guard is a “ Kon Knueppel favorite,” Stein notes, and is well-liked in Charlotte. Still, there are no other obvious release candidates on the Hornets’ roster.
 Powell, meanwhile, has a partial guarantee of $1MM that would increase to $1.5MM on opening night and has been with the Mavs since 2014, but retaining him might require the team to part with a promising young player, such as Moussa Cisse , or someone with multiple guaranteed years left on his contract, like Caleb Martin .

 ***EXAMINING THE PLAYOFF RÉSUMÉS OF 12 NBA GREATS (post 1970) TO AID IN EACH PLAYER’s RESPECTIVE ALL-TIME RANKING***
 Exactly why is it that, of the three major professional sports leagues of the United States, the NBA, without a doubt, lays claim to boasting the greatest contrast with its regular-season product versus its post-season product? Could the so-called “Player Empowerment Era” have anything to do with it? Perhaps. Is “team tanking” far more prevalent in basketball than the other two sports? Or could it be the media chooses to cover it more in this sport? What about private equity firms entering the fray of partial team ownership? Could that be a factor as to why the NBA regular season visuals are so strikingly different than its mid-April-through-June counterpart? But doesn’t private equity ownership also exist in the NFL and MLB?
 Since most of us don’t have a foot in door, we are only left to speculate on this topic. Sure, the NBA regular season still has its moments. But there is an undeniable feeling we are continuing to trudge further and further away from the meaningfulness of winning one’s division and claiming the top seed, of the importance of rivalries to draw us all in, and the sport convincing viewers that there is more to appreciate about the league than seeing how many times your team can break the 120-point mark in a game.
 With all that said, with an increasingly watered-down version from October into April, just how logical would it be to place a GREATER importance on the regular season accolades in determining a player’s status among the all-time greats? Could it potentially make more sense to apply the metaphor and envision the regular season now as the ‘vitamins/supplements’ of a healthy lifestyle and the postseason as ‘the primary diet’?
 As a bit of a basketball historian – first becoming exposed to the sport during the Bird-Magic era – I spend way too much time thinking about the all-time player rankings. Over the summer, I thought it’d be a good idea to delve strictly into the playoff résumés of at least 10 individuals widely considered to be among the all-time greats of the NBA – more specifically, each player’s TEAM successes and failures because, after all, that’s all that really matters once the regular season ends. Players like George Mikan, Bill Russell, Wilt Chamberlain, and Jerry West just could NOT be included in this examination – less competition, and fewer playoff games/rounds back then.
 NOTE: For each of the 12 players I chose, I divided his career into 4 stages (5 for the two guys who came straight out of high school and into the league): the“raw and unrefined” stage (4 years), the “prime years” stage (8), the “seasoned and refined” stage, and the “twilight” stage (varies). For the two players with 5 stages, I entitled the first stage “teens to NBA” (2 years).
 Several numbers/percentages categories are to follow. The “BETTER HALF” are the upper tier players in that individual category, while the “LESSER HALF” are the lower tier players from that individual category.
